title: BBR Button Board
text: BBR Button Board A button box you build out of tiles. One USB cable to the Driver Station. The Button Board is a modular control panel for FIRST robotics. A main module plugs into the Driver Station laptop over USB and presents itself as a game controller. Everything a driver actually touches lives on tiles — nine-key keypads, single keys, arcade buttons, rotary encoders — daisy-chained off the main module on one four-wire cable. Build the panel you want. Tiles chain in any order. Add one mid-season without rewiring anything. No code on the robot. The board is an ordinary game controller. Your OpMode or robot code reads buttons exactly the way it reads a gamepad. Works with both Driver Stations. An FRC-friendly HID gamepad with 32 buttons, or an XInput gamepad for the FTC Driver Station — one setting, no hardware change. Configured in the browser. Bind a key by pressing it. No firmware rebuild, no config file. Keys that relabel themselves. A screen key has a colour display inside the cap, so one key can say INTAKE in one part of a match and CLIMB in another. LEDs your robot drives. Tiles with RGB keys can be lit from a companion app on the Driver Station laptop, so the panel reacts to what the robot is doing. How it fits together Driver Station laptop │ USB-C ┌────┴──────┐ RS-485, one cable per link │ main ├──── tile ──── tile ──── tile ───┤ │ module │ │ └───────────┘ terminator The main module polls every tile in turn, collects which keys are down, and sends one USB report. From the Driver Station’s point of view there is a single game controller with 32 buttons on it — it never learns that there are tiles at all. Start here If you want to Read Know what the parts are What you have Put a panel together Plugging it together Get buttons working First run Decide which key does what Binding buttons Light the panel from robot state Driver Station app Change a key’s legend mid-match Screen keys and legends Two things this board deliberately is not: it is not a keyboard, and it does not run your robot code. It is a controller the Driver Station already knows how to talk to, so nothing on the robot has to change to use one. The one exception is changing a screen key’s legend during a match, which needs a few lines in your OpMode — see Changing legends in a match.

title: What you have
text: What you have The main module One per panel. It has the USB-C socket, the processor that runs the bus, and two tile connectors. Connects to Driver Station laptop, USB-C Presents itself as A game controller — 32 buttons, 4 axes Drives Up to 31 tiles on one chain Also carries The CFG button, and jumpers for bus termination The main module holds the whole configuration: which key is which button, what colour each LED is, and which USB personality to use. Tiles hold none of it, which is why a tile can be swapped for an identical one without reconfiguring anything. The tiles Every tile is the same on the bus — a small processor, a transceiver, and two connectors — and differs only in what a person touches. Tile What it is Keys mx9 3 × 3 grid of Cherry MX hot-swap keys 9 mx9rgb The same, with an RGB LED under every key 9 mx1 A single MX key 1 arc4 Four arcade buttons, each on a 3-pin JST PH lead 4 enc2 Two rotary encoders with push-to-click shafts 2 encoders + 2 keys disp1 A 128 × 32 text panel — a readout, not a control none screenkey1 One key whose cap is a 128 × 128 colour screen 1 disp1 and screenkey1 are the display tiles: the panel shows what the robot is doing, and on screenkey1 it is the key’s own legend, so the label changes as the match does. See Screen keys and legends. Keys on a tile are numbered from 0. Buttons the Driver Station sees are numbered from 1. Those two numbering schemes are separate on purpose — see Binding buttons. Hot-swap means the key switches push in and pull out by hand, with no soldering. A broken switch in the pit is a ten-second repair. The terminators Two per panel, one at each end of the chain, each on a short cable into the spare connector there. They are not tiles: a small 20 mm board with one connector and one resistor on it, and no electronics. The single connector is deliberate — a terminator cannot be cabled through, so it can only ever sit at an end. They matter more than they look. A chain with no terminators still works on a short cable and starts dropping tiles on a long one, which is the kind of fault that only shows up at a competition. Fit both and forget about it — see Plugging it together. What you supply A USB-C cable to the Driver Station laptop. That is the only power the panel needs. Tile cables — one per link in the chain, six-way JST GH, straight through. Key switches and keycaps for the MX tiles, or arcade buttons for arc4. Any Cherry MX-compatible switch fits. What the Driver Station sees Personality Driver Station You get frc FRC (Windows) 32 buttons and 4 axes on one HID gamepad xinput FTC (Driver Hub / phone) An Xbox-360-style gamepad; the 32 buttons map onto its controls This is a setting, not a different board. Change it in the config app, unplug, plug back in. See The config app.

title: Plugging it together
text: Plugging it together The chain Every board — the main module and every tile — has two identical connectors, wired in parallel. Run a cable from one board to the next in any order you like: main module ──── mx9 ──── mx9 ──── enc2 │ │ terminator terminator Order does not matter. The main module finds tiles by asking, not by counting along the cable. Both connectors on a board are the same. There is no “in” and no “out”. Cables are straight through. Pin 1 to pin 1. There is no crossover cable in this system. Up to 31 tiles, and up to about 4 m of cable in total. Terminators go at both ends The two connectors that end up with nothing plugged into them — one on the main module, one on the last tile — each take a terminator. Fit both. A chain missing a terminator usually works on the bench and then loses tiles under vibration or on a longer cable, which reads as a key that “sometimes doesn’t work” rather than as a wiring fault. If your panel is permanently installed and the main module sits at one end of the chain, you can use the main module’s built-in termination jumper instead of a terminator in its spare connector. One or the other, not both. Power The whole panel runs off the USB cable. There is nothing else to plug in. That budget is not unlimited, and LEDs are what spend it. The main module works out the worst-case draw of every tile on the chain and turns the global LED brightness down until the panel fits the budget — so an over-lit panel dims rather than browning out mid-match. If you are running from a port that can supply more than the default, raise the budget in the config app. See LED colours. Adding a tile mid-season Plug it into a spare connector, moving the terminator to the new end of the chain. The main module gives it an address by itself the next time it is powered on. Nothing that was already bound changes. The one thing to know: bindings are stored per tile position, not per physical board. If you swap a faulty tile for an identical one, the replacement inherits the old one’s bindings automatically. If you add a second tile of the same kind, it is a new tile and starts unbound. Binding buttons covers what to do when the board cannot tell which case it is looking at. Cable pinout Six-way JST GH, 1.25 mm pitch. You only need this if you are making cables. Pin Signal 1 GND 2 GND 3 B (−) 4 A (+) 5 5 V 6 5 V Ground and 5 V are doubled to carry the current an illuminated arcade tile can draw. The differential pair sits in the middle, away from the power pins.

title: First run
headings: 3. Check the board sees your tiles
6. Point the Driver Station at it
text: First run Ten minutes, start to finish: plug in, bind a key, watch it register. 1. Plug it in Connect the tiles into a chain, fit the two terminators, and plug the main module into your laptop with a USB-C cable. The power LED comes on immediately. The laptop should find a new game controller by itself — no driver, no install. On Windows, joy.cpl (Start → Run → joy.cpl) shows it and is a useful sanity check throughout. 2. Open the config app Go to the config site in Chrome or Edge and press Connect. The browser shows a list of serial ports; pick the Button Board. Chromium browsers only. The config app talks to the board over Web Serial, which Firefox and Safari do not implement. The page will tell you rather than failing silently. The Connect screen then shows what the board is: firmware version, serial number, how many tiles it can see, and which USB personality is active. 3. Check the board sees your tiles Switch to Diagnose. Every tile in the chain should be listed as online, with the tile kind and how many keys it has. If a tile is missing, work through Troubleshooting — but check the obvious two first: a cable not clicked fully home, and a missing terminator. Press keys. Diagnose shows presses live, straight off the bus, before any binding is involved. This is the fastest way to prove a switch works. 4. Bind a key Go to Configure. The chain is down the left; pick a tile and it is drawn the way it physically is, keys in the right places. Click the key you want to bind. In the inspector, choose the logical button it should be — 1 to 32. Press the key. The board confirms it. That is the whole binding step. Repeat for as many keys as you need. Buttons you never bind simply never press. 5. Save Press Save. Until you do, the configuration lives in RAM and is lost on the next power cycle. Saved configuration survives unplugging, reboots and firmware updates of the tiles. 6. Point the Driver Station at it FRC: the board appears as a 32-button joystick. Assign it a port in the Driver Station the way you would any joystick. FTC: switch the USB personality to xinput on the Connect screen, then unplug and plug back in — the personality only changes at a USB reset. The Driver Hub then sees an Xbox-style gamepad, and Start+A / Start+B binds it as gamepad 1 or 2 as usual. Nothing works and nothing shows up? Hold the CFG button on the main module while you plug the USB cable in. That forces a known-good configuration personality regardless of what is stored, so a board can never be configured into being unreachable. Testing without a robot The Diagnose screen can make the board report button presses that no one is touching — one button at a time walking 1 → 32, one button held, or all of them at once. That lets you prove the Driver Station end of the chain works before any tile is bound, and prove a binding reaches the robot without needing a third hand. Test mode ends by itself when you disconnect, so it cannot be left on by accident.

title: Updating the firmware
text: Updating the firmware Two different things get updated, in two different ways. Both live on the Firmware screen of the config app. Tiles Tiles update over the bus — the same cable they are already plugged into. Nothing is unplugged, no programmer is needed, and one tile updates at a time while the rest of the chain carries on. Open Firmware in the config app. Any tile running older firmware than the images the site carries is listed with an Update button. Press it and wait. Progress is shown as it goes. The tile drops out of the chain for a few seconds and rejoins when it is done. Its address and its bindings are untouched. A tile that loses power partway through an update is not bricked. The updater writes to a staging area and only commits after the whole image has arrived and its checksum matches; a tile that never gets that far comes back on its old firmware. The main module The main module updates over USB, using the same drag-and-drop mechanism as any RP2040 board. Press Update main module in the config app. The board reboots into its bootloader, and the COM port disappears — this is expected, and the config app will tell you it has lost the connection. A USB drive called RPI-RP2 appears on your computer. Drag the .uf2 file onto it. The drive disappears and the board restarts on the new firmware. Your configuration — bindings, LED colours, USB personality — is stored separately from the firmware and survives the update. If the config app cannot reach the board at all, you can get to the same place by hand: unplug the board, hold the BOOTSEL button, plug it back in, and release. RPI-RP2 appears the same way. Which versions am I on? The Connect screen reports the main module’s firmware version, and Diagnose reports each tile’s. Mixed versions across tiles are fine — the board checks that every tile speaks a compatible protocol and flags any that does not, rather than assuming.

title: The config app
text: The config app Everything is configured in a browser. There is nothing to install, and the page talks to the board directly over USB — your configuration never leaves the laptop. Chrome or Edge, on a desktop. The app uses Web Serial, which Firefox and Safari do not implement and which no mobile browser supports. It has to be served over HTTPS or from localhost; opening the files directly with file:// will not work. Press Connect, pick the board from the browser’s port list, and you are in. The board has to be selected by hand the first time — a page cannot go looking for serial ports on its own, which is exactly the protection you want. Four screens Connect Board identity: product, firmware version, serial number, tile count, and whether the stored configuration is valid. This is also where the USB personality is set — frc for the FRC Driver Station, xinput for FTC. The change is stored immediately but only takes effect on the next USB reset, so unplug and plug back in after switching. Configure The panel as it physically is. The chain runs down the left; select a tile and it is drawn in its real layout, so you click the key you mean instead of hunting through a table of numbers. Selecting a key opens the inspector, which does three things: binds it to a logical button, adds it to a group with other keys, and sets its LED colour. See Binding buttons and LED colours. Select a display tile and the inspector offers what that tile can do instead: text and a bar on the panel, a Picture to send or store, the tile’s Slots, and the Legend codes that let robot code switch between them. See Screen keys and legends. Diagnose What the bus is actually doing. Tiles — every tile the board knows about, its kind, its firmware, whether it is online, and which keys are down right now. Counters — checksum errors and missed replies per tile. Both should sit at zero; a tile that is steadily accumulating either has a cable or termination problem. Power — the LED power budget, the worst-case draw of the current panel, and the brightness that fits it. Test — makes the board report button presses with no tile involved, for checking the Driver Station end on its own. Firmware Updates for the tiles over the bus, and for the main module over USB. See Updating the firmware. Saved versus not saved Changes take effect immediately — bind a key and it works on the next press — but they live in RAM until you press Save. The app shows when there are unsaved changes. That split is deliberate: you can try a layout, decide you preferred the old one, and power-cycle back to it. Without a board The config app runs against a built-in fake board with a few tiles on it, so the interface can be explored, demonstrated or taught with nothing plugged in.

title: Binding buttons
headings: Keys, buttons, and why they are different
What happens when a tile disappears
text: Binding buttons Keys, buttons, and why they are different A key is a physical thing on a tile. Keys are numbered from 0 within their tile, and a key on its own does nothing. A logical button is what the Driver Station sees. There are 32 of them, numbered 1 to 32, and they exist whether or not anything is bound to them. Binding connects the two. Until a key is bound, pressing it registers nowhere. This indirection is the whole point. Your robot code refers to Button 7, and stays true when Button 7 moves to a different key, a different tile, or a different kind of tile entirely. Binding a key In Configure, click the key, choose a button number, and press the key to confirm. The board waits for the press itself, so there is no way to bind the wrong key by mistyping a number. Rebinding a key to a different button replaces the old binding, including any combo the key was part of. Groups: several keys, one button Several keys can feed the same button. The button is pressed while any of them is down. This is what you want for: The same action reachable from two ends of a wide panel. A driver and a co-driver who each need the same override. An arcade button and a keypad key that do the same job. Add a key to an existing button rather than replacing it, and up to 16 keys can share one button. Combos: one key, several buttons The reverse works too. One key can press several buttons at once, and releasing it releases them all together. The case that needs it is FTC. The Driver Station assigns a pad to gamepad 1 when it sees Start+A, and to gamepad 2 on Start+B. That normally takes two hands. Bind one key to each and it takes one press. In Configure, click the key, then: Start+A or Start+B sets that combo in one click. Combo turns on toggling: each number you click is added to the key, or taken off it. Click Combo again to go back to picking one button. The key shows every button it feeds, for example B1+8. A combo does not take the buttons away from other keys: a key bound to Start+A and a separate key bound to Start both work. If the buttons in a combo have different LED colours, the key shows the colour of the lowest-numbered one. The Driver Station sees every button in a combo change in the same instant. It does not see Start first and then A. The board sends the combo correctly, but whether the Driver Hub accepts simultaneous presses has not been tested on one yet. If it does not, bind Start and A to two separate keys as before. Debounce Mechanical switches make and break contact several times in the few milliseconds around a press. The tile filters that out, and the default — 5 ms — suits every switch these tiles are designed for. You can raise it per tile if a particular switch chatters, at the cost of that much latency on every press. Worn arcade microswitches are the usual reason. What happens when a tile disappears If a tile stops answering — cable pulled, board damaged — every button bound to it reads as released, immediately. Not “stuck at whatever it was last”, which is the failure mode that drives a robot into a wall. Bindings to a missing tile are kept, not deleted, so unplugging a tile to work on the panel and plugging it back in costs you nothing. Swapping and replacing tiles Bindings are stored against a tile’s position on the bus, and the board remembers which physical tile was in each position. Replace a broken tile with an identical one — the new tile takes the old one’s place and its bindings, automatically. Add another tile of the same kind — it is a new tile, and starts unbound. When the board cannot tell those two cases apart, it says so instead of guessing, and the config app offers the choice. Nothing is silently rebound. Saving Bindings work as soon as they are made, but live in RAM until you press Save. Save writes them to flash and reads them back to check.

title: LED colours
headings: Colours follow the button, not the key
text: LED colours Tiles with RGB keys — mx9rgb today — have one addressable LED under every key. There are two independent ways to drive them, and understanding which is which saves a lot of confusion. Two layers Defaults are part of your saved configuration. They are what the panel looks like when it powers up: a red key for the emergency stop, blue for the intake, dark for everything unbound. Set them in the config app’s Configure screen, and press Save. The live layer is set at runtime, over USB, by a companion app on the Driver Station laptop. It is never saved. This is what makes a panel react — flash the arm button red while the arm is out of bounds, light the scoring buttons only when the robot is in range. In FTC mode there is no USB channel for a companion app, but the robot can still write the live layer: a rumble code can be set up to recolour keys. See Changing a key’s colour the same way. The live layer wins wherever both are set, per LED. Clearing it returns every LED to the saved defaults. See Driver Station app for how to write to it. Colours follow the button, not the key An LED colour set for a logical button moves with that button. Rebind Button 7 to a different key and its colour goes with it — which is almost always what you meant. LEDs that are not under a bound key — edge glow, spare positions — are addressed by tile and LED number instead. Effects Effect What it does solid On, steady. The default. blink Slow flash fast Fast flash breathe Smooth fade in and out Effects are generated on the tile, so a blink stays smooth no matter how busy the bus is, and a companion app does not have to send anything to keep it going. Press feedback By default a key flashes white while it is held, over whatever colour it was showing. It is a small thing that makes a panel feel like it is working — and on a panel where several keys share a button, it shows which one was actually pressed. You can change the feedback colour, or turn it off per button. Brightness and the power budget The whole panel runs off the USB cable, and LEDs are what spend that budget. Rather than let a big panel brown out, the main module adds up the worst-case draw of every tile on the chain and lowers the global brightness until the total fits the budget. So adding a fourth lit tile dims the panel slightly instead of destabilising it. The Diagnose → Power view shows all three numbers: the budget, the worst case, and the brightness actually in use. If you are running from a port that can supply more than the default, raise the budget there. If a panel cannot fit even at minimum brightness, the board holds the LEDs off and raises a fault rather than trying. The Power view says so. Turning everything off There is a single “all LEDs off” command, and it takes priority over anything else in flight. It is the right thing to reach for when a panel is doing something unexpected on a field.

title: Rotary encoders
text: Rotary encoders The enc2 tile carries two rotary encoders, each with a push-to-click shaft. They are the right control for anything continuous — arm setpoint, shooter speed, LED brightness on the robot — where a button can only step. Encoder tiles are the newest part of the system. The protocol and the config app support them; the tile firmware is still in development. Everything on this page describes the design, not something you can plug in today. What the Driver Station sees FRC. Each encoder can be bound to one of four axes. The axis reports an accumulated position — turn it clockwise and the number goes up, keep turning and it keeps going. Four axes is the whole board, so two enc2 tiles claim all of them. An axis is not a joystick. It does not spring back to centre and it has no deadzone, because there is nothing to return to: the value is where the knob has got to. Scale sets how far one click moves the axis. The default, 256, makes every click one step your robot code can see: the Driver Station sends axes to the robot at 8 bits, so smaller values need several clicks before anything changes. At 256 the axis reaches its end after about 128 clicks, around six turns of a typical knob. Pick a larger scale for a knob that should reach the end in fewer turns. Changing the scale zeroes the position. FTC. XInput’s sticks are sprung and deadzoned, which throws away an accumulated position entirely. So under xinput an encoder becomes pulsed buttons instead: one button pulses per detent clockwise, another per detent anticlockwise, and your OpMode counts them. Pulsed buttons are available under frc too, if you would rather count clicks than read a position. The shaft push The push switch on each encoder is an ordinary key. Bind it like any other key — it takes a logical button number and behaves exactly as a keypad key does. Zeroing An accumulated position needs a defined starting point. The board can zero any axis, or all of them, on command — at the start of a match, or when the mechanism it drives is homed.

title: Screen keys and legends
headings: Text is cheap, pictures are not
Loading a picture into a slot
Getting them there from a terminal
Why the indirection is worth it
text: Screen keys and legends Most keys have a legend printed on the cap, and changing it means pulling the cap off. A screen key has a colour display inside the cap, so the legend is software — the same physical key can say INTAKE in one part of a match and CLIMB in another. Screen keys are the newest part of the system, and further from your hands than the encoder tiles are. The protocol, the config app and the tile firmware all support them; the board has never been manufactured, and nothing on this page has run on real hardware. Everything here describes the design and works against the config app’s built-in fake board. The two display tiles Tile Panel Keys disp1 128 × 32 monochrome, 21 columns × 4 rows of text none — it is a readout, not a control screenkey1 128 × 128 colour, inside a key cap 1 disp1 is the panel you put on the panel: match time, a mechanism state, a message from the robot. screenkey1 is one key whose cap is the screen. Both are ordinary tiles on the same chain, in any order, and both are addressed like any other. Text is cheap, pictures are not A display tile holds a grid of characters, not a picture. The board sends text and the tile draws it with its own font. That is what keeps a screen tile affordable in bus time — a line of text is a few dozen bytes. A picture is a different matter. A 128 × 128 full-colour image is 32 KB, which is a couple of seconds of bus with everything else waiting. So there are two ways to put one on a panel, and choosing between them is the whole of this page: Stream it Store it in a slot Colours Two, dithered Full colour Cost to show ~0.2 s of bus, every time One frame — a few milliseconds Cost to load none seconds, once Kept where nowhere; the panel holds it until cleared the tile’s own flash chip Streaming is right for something you show once. Storing is what makes a legend work, and it is the reason a screen key can be in colour at all: the picture only has to cross the bus at configuration time, so the bus objection to 16-bit colour disappears. After that, changing legends is as cheap as changing a light. A screenkey1 has room for several stored pictures. Each numbered place is a slot. Loading a picture into a slot In the config app’s Configure screen, select the tile and find the Picture section of the inspector. Choose an image file. The app shows you what the tile will actually draw — re-sized and encoded for that panel — not the file you picked. Set send as to a stored picture. Choose the slot and, on a colour panel, the encoding. Full colour is rgb565; the one-bit form is smaller and faster to load. Press Store in slot n. The slot is erased the moment the transfer starts and is not a picture again until the whole thing arrives and its checksum matches. So an interrupted store leaves the slot empty, never half-drawn. If it fails, the app says so and you store it again. The Slots section lists what is in each one, with Show and Erase buttons for checking your work. What a slot holds cannot be read back — there is no command that asks. The list in the config app is what that page put there, not what the tile reports. Close the tab and it forgets; the pictures stay on the tile. Binding legend codes A stored picture is switched by a number, and that number is what robot code sends. The Legend codes section of the same inspector binds them. There are fifteen codes, 1 to 15. Each row picks a slot on this tile: Code Bound to 1 slot 0 — intake.png 2 slot 3 — climb.png 3 unbound A code with no binding does nothing. So does a binding whose tile is unplugged or whose slot is empty — a match is not the place to pop up a configuration error. Zero is never a legend. Zero is how the robot stops a rumble, and stopping a rumble must not change what is on a screen. Bindings are part of your saved configuration, so press Save when you are happy with them. Why the indirection is worth it A code does not name a key and it does not name a picture. It names an entry in the map, which says which tile and which slot. That means the layout can change without the robot code changing. Move the legend to a different key, swap the picture for a better one, rearrange the panel between matches — the OpMode still says “show code 3”, and code 3 is whatever you have most recently decided it means. Getting them there from a terminal Everything above is also a command on the serial channel, if you would rather script it: python3 tools/bbctl.py --rumble-list # what is bound now python3 tools/bbctl.py --rumble-bind 3 5 0 # code 3 → tile 5, slot 0 Loading a picture is disp <addr> slot <n> begin/data/end, which tools/bb wraps. Next Once the pictures are stored and the codes are bound, the robot can switch between them mid-match — see Changing legends in a match.

title: Changing legends in a match
headings: The number is a legend code, not a key
Changing a key’s colour the same way
There is no way to blank a key
If the board is unplugged mid-match
Do not use it as an animation
text: Changing legends in a match A screen key can show a different legend as the match goes on — INTAKE while you are collecting, SCORE while you are lined up, CLIMB in the endgame. This page is how the robot tells it to. It is the one place the Button Board asks for code on the robot. Everything else about the board is an ordinary gamepad. This describes the design, not something you can plug in today. The screenkey1 tile has never been manufactured, and it has not been established that the FTC Driver Station forwards a rumble call to this board at all. The library is written, tested against both ends of the arithmetic, and unproven on hardware. Read What is not proven before you rely on it in a real match. Why rumble, of all things For FTC the board presents itself as an Xbox-style gamepad, and that leaves it with exactly one interface — no serial port, no config channel. During a match there is no way in. Except one. The Driver Station can send a gamepad a rumble command, and gamepad.rumble() is a normal thing for an OpMode to call. That is a very narrow door: it carries a number, not text. But a stored picture is switched by a number, so the number is all we need. The trade is: load the legends before the match, switch them during it with one call. The number is a legend code, not a key showLegend(3) does not mean “key 3”. It means “whatever the config app has bound to code 3” — see Binding legend codes. Name the codes in your OpMode for what they mean, and the numbers appear in exactly one place: static final int LEGEND_INTAKE = 1; static final int LEGEND_SCORE = 2; static final int LEGEND_CLIMB = 3; Someone can then rearrange the panel — a different key, a different picture — without anyone touching the robot code. Adding the library FTC teams copy files; there is no dependency to add beyond the SDK you already have. From the repository: cp -r robot/ftc/src/org TeamCode/src/main/java/ cp -r robot/ftc/src-ftc/org TeamCode/src/main/java/ That leaves three files in org/firstinspires/ftc/teamcode/buttonboard/. Do not copy test/ — it is for a desktop JDK and Android Studio will try to build it. If your team uses a different package root, change the package line in all three files to match. The rumble API landed in FTC SDK v7.0; nothing here needs anything newer. A minimal OpMode @TeleOp(name = "Button Board legends") public class LegendDemo extends LinearOpMode { static final int LEGEND_INTAKE = 1; static final int LEGEND_SCORE = 2; static final int LEGEND_CLIMB = 3; @Override public void runOpMode() { // gamepad1 must be the pad the Button Board bound as. ButtonBoard board = new ButtonBoard(new GamepadRumbleSink(gamepad1)); waitForStart(); while (opModeIsActive()) { // Safe to call every loop: it sends only when the code changes. if (gamepad1.right_trigger > 0.5) { board.showLegend(LEGEND_CLIMB); } else if (gamepad1.a) { board.showLegend(LEGEND_SCORE); } else { board.showLegend(LEGEND_INTAKE); } telemetry.addData("legend", board.lastLegend()); telemetry.update(); } } } The config app writes this call out for you: the Legend codes section has an In the OpMode block with the exact line for every code you have bound, and a Copy button. The API Call Does showLegend(int code) Show the legend bound to code — unless it is already the last one sent. Returns whether it sent anything. Throws on anything outside 1–15. refresh() Send the last code again regardless. For when the board was power-cycled and your belief about it is stale. forget() Drop that belief without sending. The next showLegend sends whatever it is given. lastLegend() The last code sent — not what the board is known to be showing. stopRumble() Send zero power. Stops a real gamepad buzzing; does not clear the key. Call it every loop showLegend() remembers what it last sent and suppresses repeats, which is the entire reason to use it rather than calling rumble() yourself. An OpMode loop runs at about 50 Hz, and the SDK’s own sample is blunt about not spamming the rumble motors. So write it as a plain statement of what the legend should be right now, and let it work out whether anything needs sending. There is no way to blank a key Zero is the SDK’s stop, so the board ignores it — deliberately, because ending a rumble must not wipe a screen. To show nothing, store a blank picture in a slot, bind a code to it, and show that code. If the board is unplugged mid-match Nothing tells you. There is no acknowledgement on this path at all: a board in FTC mode cannot answer. If it is power-cycled it comes back showing whatever its map starts with, while your OpMode still believes the legend it last sent — so the next showLegend() of that same code is suppressed as a repeat and the panel stays wrong. refresh() is the way out, wired to a button you can reach. Do not use it as an animation The SDK keeps one outgoing rumble at a time and sends it about every 50 ms. Two calls inside one of those windows means the first is thrown away, not queued. That is harmless here, because a code names a legend absolutely — the panel converges on the latest one you asked for. What it costs is intermediate legends: flick A → B → C inside 50 ms and B may never appear. If a legend needs to be seen, leave it up for at least a tenth of a second. Rumble goes to one gamepad. Whichever position the Driver Station gave the board — gamepad1 or gamepad2 — is the one to construct GamepadRumbleSink with. Send to the other and nothing happens, with no error. Changing a key’s colour the same way A code can also recolour keys. In the config app, select a key on an RGB tile, and under Robot colour pick a code, an effect and a colour. When the robot sends that code, the key takes that colour. If the same code also has a legend bound, one showLegend() call changes both, so a key can turn red and read CLIMB at the same moment. There are two special colours. ∅ turns the LED off. normal puts the key back on the colour it has in your saved configuration. A code changes only the keys it names. Because the SDK can drop a code sent less than 50 ms before the next one, don’t rely on an in-between code having arrived. If code 5 means “back to normal”, give code 5 a normal entry for every key your other codes recolour. These colours live on the board’s live LED layer, the same one the Driver Station app writes. They are not saved, and a power cycle or led reset clears them. That brings the same problem as an unplugged board above: showLegend() thinks the colour is still showing, so refresh() is the way to put it back. The map holds up to 32 robot colours in total. Setting the board up first The codes mean nothing until the pictures are on the tile and the codes are bound, and neither can be done in FTC mode — that is the whole reason this channel exists. The order is: Put the board in a mode that has the config channel: frc in the config app’s Connect screen. Save, then unplug and plug back in. Load the pictures into slots and bind the codes. Add any robot colours. Save. Switch back to xinput, save, unplug and plug back in. Check which gamepad position the Driver Station gives it. The bindings live in your saved configuration, so step 2 survives step 3. The config app offers a “bind the next code” button that waits for a rumble and binds whichever code arrives. Against a real board it will wait forever. No single board can both receive a rumble and report that it did — the mode with the rumble endpoint has no config channel to report on. It works against the fake board, and it becomes real if the two are ever combined. Bind by picking the number instead; that works everywhere. What is not proven None of this has run on hardware, and it is worth being precise about which parts are assumptions: No part of this path has been tested on a real board — not the OpMode, not the Driver Station’s forwarding, not the board’s decoding of a real rumble packet. That the Driver Station forwards a rumble to this board is not established. What has been tested is only that an FTC Driver Hub recognises the board as a gamepad. Whether its rumble path reaches a device with this board’s identity is exactly the open question. The ~50 ms rate limit is read out of the SDK’s source, not measured. Latency is unknown. Showing a stored picture takes about a frame at the tile, but the time from showLegend() to pixels also includes the Driver Station, the radio link and the bus, and none of it has been timed. isRumbling() will say true for the length of each step even though the board has no motors to rumble. Do not gate legend changes on it — you would suppress real ones.

title: Install the library
text: Install the library The Button Board can be driven from a program on the Driver Station laptop — reading robot state from NetworkTables and pushing LED colours and display text back to the panel. bb is the Python library for that. You do not need this to use the board. Buttons work through the Driver Station like any gamepad, with nothing installed. This is for making the panel react to the robot. What you need Python 3.9 or newer. pyserial. python3 -m pip install pyserial The library itself lives in tools/bb/ in the repository. Copy that directory next to your script, or put its parent on PYTHONPATH: export PYTHONPATH=/path/to/BBRControlBoard/tools Check it works from bb import Board with Board.open() as board: # finds the COM port by itself print(board.hello()) {'ok': True, 'product': 'Button Board', 'fw': '0.1.0', 'proto': 1, ...} If it cannot find the board, pass the port explicitly — Board.open(port="COM7") on Windows, Board.open(port="/dev/ttyACM0") on Linux. Without a board MockBoard speaks the same protocol in-process, so a companion app can be written and tested with no hardware attached: from bb import MockBoard board = MockBoard() board.led(3, "red") print(board.state.leds) # {('btn', 3): 'led 3 FF0000'} One connection at a time The board’s configuration channel is a serial port, and a serial port has one owner. If the config app has the board open in a browser tab, your script cannot open it, and the other way round. Close one before starting the other.

title: Your first script
text: Your first script A companion app is a loop: read what the robot is doing, decide what the panel should look like, push it. Here is the whole shape of one. from bb import Board with Board.open() as board: leds = board.led_layer() while True: arm_fault = read_from_networktables("arm_fault") in_range = read_from_networktables("in_scoring_range") leds.set(3, "red" if arm_fault else "off") leds.set(7, "green" if in_range else "off", fx="breathe") leds.flush() Why led_layer() and not board.led() Both work. The difference is what happens when nothing changes. board.led(3, "red") sends a command every time you call it. In a 50 Hz loop that is 50 commands a second per button, whether or not the colour changed — the board processes all of them and puts the changes on the bus. led_layer() stages the writes and flush() sends only what changed. A steady panel costs nothing at all. Use it for anything that runs in a loop; use board.led() for one-off changes. leds.set(3, "red") leds.flush() # sends: led 3 FF0000 leds.set(3, "red") leds.flush() # sends nothing Colours Anything sensible works: leds.set(1, "red") # a name leds.set(2, "#0040FF") # hex, with or without the # leds.set(3, (0, 64, 255)) # an (r, g, b) triple leds.set(4, 0x0040FF) # an int leds.set(5, None) # off Named colours include red green blue yellow cyan magenta orange purple pink amber lime teal white off, plus alliance_red and alliance_blue. Effects leds.set(3, "red", "blink") # slow flash leds.set(3, "red", "fast") # fast flash leds.set(3, "red", "breathe") # fade in and out The tile generates the effect, so it keeps running with no further commands. Clearing up board.led_reset() # back to the colours saved in the configuration board.led_all("off") # everything dark, right now led_all("off") is the panic button — it takes priority over anything else in progress. When the board goes away A companion app runs for a whole match, and USB cables get kicked. Every call raises rather than failing quietly: from bb import Board, BoardError try: leds.flush() except BoardError as e: print("lost the panel:", e) # reconnect, then leds.forget() so the next flush redraws everything forget() matters after a reconnect or a reboot: the diffing layer thinks the board still shows what it last sent, and after a power cycle that is no longer true.

title: Python API summary
text: Python API summary Everything here is a method on Board. Each one sends a command and returns the board’s reply as a dictionary, or raises. Connecting Call What it does Board.open(port=None) Open the board, auto-detecting the port board.close() Close it. Also happens on leaving a with block MockBoard() An in-process board, no hardware Identity and state Call Returns board.hello() Product, firmware version, serial, tile count, USB personality board.tiles() A list, one entry per tile: kind, firmware, state, keys currently down board.tile(addr) One tile’s entry, or None board.stats() Uptime, poll cycle time, fault state, LED power budget LEDs Call What it does board.led(btn, colour, fx=None, press=None) Set a logical button’s colour board.led_tile(addr, index, colour, fx=None) Set one LED by tile and position board.led_all(colour) Every LED on every tile board.led_reset() Back to the saved defaults board.led_layer() A diffing writer — see Your first script colour takes a name, "#RRGGBB", "RRGGBB", an (r, g, b) triple, an int, or None for off. fx is "solid", "blink", "fast" or "breathe". press turns the white press-flash on or off for that button. LedLayer Call What it does layer.set(btn, colour, fx, press) Stage a colour layer.set_tile(addr, index, colour, fx) Stage a colour by tile and position layer.flush() Send what changed; returns how many commands went out layer.all(colour) / layer.reset() Send immediately and reset the diff layer.forget() Force the next flush() to resend everything Bindings Call What it does board.bind(btn, add=False) Wait for a key press and bind it. add=True joins a group board.bind_cancel() Stop waiting board.unbind(btn) Remove every key from a button board.unbind(btn, addr, key) Remove one key from a group board.map_get() / board.map_set(m) The whole configuration as a dictionary board.save() Write it to flash bind() blocks until someone presses a key, up to 30 seconds. Encoders Call What it does board.bind_axis(n) Bind axis 1–4 to the next encoder turned board.unbind_axis(n) Remove it board.enc_zero(n=None) Zero one axis, or all of them Display tiles Call What it does board.screen(addr) A row-diffing writer for a display tile screen.text(row, s) / screen.bar(row, col, width, value) Stage a row screen.flush() Send changed rows and commit them together screen.clear() Blank the panel The first display tile is disp1: a 128×32 SSD1306, 21 columns × 4 rows. Take the geometry from screen.cols / screen.rows, which come from the tile’s own descriptor, rather than hard-coding it. No disp1 board has been built yet, so develop against MockBoard(); MockBoard(display=False) reproduces a board older than §14, which answers unknown. The board itself Call What it does board.usb("frc") / board.usb("xinput") Set the USB personality; takes effect at the next reset board.power_budget(mA) Set the LED power budget board.test("walk", 250) / board.test("off") Report button presses with no tile involved board.reset() / board.reset(factory=True) Reboot, optionally erasing the configuration Events The board reports things that happen on its own — a tile lost, a fault raised, a key pressed during binding. def on_tile(ev): print(ev["addr"], ev["state"]) # 3 lost unsubscribe = board.on("tile", on_tile) Names are tile, fault, key, enc, progress and player; "*" receives all of them. Callbacks run on the library’s reader thread. Do not call board methods from inside one — the reader is what completes them, so the call blocks until it times out. Put the event on a queue and handle it in your loop. Errors Exception When CommandError The board refused the command. .err is the reason code Timeout No reply in time NotConnected The port is closed or the cable went away NoBoardFound Auto-detection could not identify a board BoardError Base class for all of the above

title: Serial command reference
text: Serial command reference The board’s configuration channel is a plain text serial port. Anything that can open a COM port can drive it — the config app, the Python library, or PuTTY in the pit with no software installed at all. You send one command per line, ending in a newline. The board answers with one JSON object per line. Every command produces exactly one final line, either {"ok":true,...} or {"ok":false,"err":"..."}. The board may send event lines at any time, marked with "ev". A client has to expect one between its own command and the reply. Baud rate is ignored; any setting works. Enter must send a newline, not a carriage return. PuTTY’s default sends CR, which this channel ignores — so commands appear to be accepted and nothing at all happens. Set it to send LF, or use bbctl. The commands Command What it does hello Identify the board: firmware, serial, tile count, USB personality tiles Every tile the board knows about stats Uptime, poll cycle time, fault state, power budget usb frc | usb xinput Set the USB personality, applied at the next reset pixel on | pixel off Flash the main module’s light white on every button press. On by default; save keeps the setting bind <btn> Wait for a key press and bind it to that button bind <btn> add Same, but add to the button’s group instead of replacing bind cancel Stop waiting unbind <btn> Remove every key from a button unbind <btn> <addr> <key> Remove one key from a group bind axis <n> Bind axis 1–4 to the next encoder turned unbind axis <n> Remove it enc zero [<n>] Zero one encoder axis, or all of them map get The whole configuration as JSON map set <json> Replace it save Write configuration to flash and verify it led <btn> <rgb> [fx] [press] Live colour for a logical button led tile <addr> <led> <rgb> [fx] Live colour by tile and LED number led all <rgb> Every LED. led all off is the panic button led reset Discard the live layer; back to saved defaults power budget <mA> Set the LED power budget test walk [ms] Press buttons 1→32 in turn, with no tile involved test hold <btn> Hold one button test all Every button at once test off Stop disp <addr> … Write text, a bar or a picture to a display tile disp <addr> slot <n> … Store, show or erase one of the tile’s saved pictures replace <old> <new> Move a tile’s bindings to another address by hand reset Reboot reset factory Erase the configuration and reboot boot Reboot into the USB bootloader for a firmware update rgb is six hex digits or off. fx is solid, blink, fast or breathe. Addresses are 1–31, logical buttons 1–32, keys count from 0. Events Event When tile A tile went online, was lost, was assigned an address, or entered its bootloader fault The fault indicator changed, with the reason key A key was pressed — only while waiting for a binding enc An encoder was turned — only while waiting for a binding progress During a tile firmware update player The FTC Driver Station assigned this board a player number rumble A rumble packet arrived, with the legend code it decodes to — FTC mode only A client that only wants request and response can ignore every line containing "ev". A worked example > hello < {"ok":true,"product":"Button Board","fw":"0.1.0","proto":1,"tiles":3,"mode":"run","usb":"frc"} > bind 7 < {"ev":"key","addr":1,"key":4} < {"ok":true,"btn":7,"addr":1,"key":4,"sources":1} > led 7 FF8800 blink < {"ok":true} > save < {"ok":true,"saved":true} bbctl tools/bbctl.py in the repository is a console for this channel that gets the details right — newline endings, holding the port open so test mode survives, and reading on past event lines to the real reply. python3 tools/bbctl.py # interactive console python3 tools/bbctl.py hello stats # run and exit python3 tools/bbctl.py -p COM7 "test walk 250" # explicit port

title: Troubleshooting
headings: Nothing appears when I plug it in
The config app cannot see the board
A tile is missing from the chain
Buttons stick on, or fire on their own
Is the board sending my presses at all?
The Driver Station sees the wrong thing
LEDs are dimmer than I set them
text: Troubleshooting Nothing appears when I plug it in Try a different USB cable. Charge-only cables are common and carry no data. Check the power LED on the main module. Dark means it is not getting power. Hold the CFG button while plugging in. That forces a known-good USB configuration whatever is stored, and is the way back from a board that was configured into being unreachable. If it still does nothing, hold BOOTSEL while plugging in. An RPI-RP2 drive appearing means the hardware is alive and the firmware is the problem — see Updating the firmware. The config app cannot see the board Are you in Chrome or Edge? Firefox and Safari have no Web Serial, and no version of the app will work in them. Is something else holding the port? A serial terminal, another browser tab, or a running Python script will each keep the port to itself. Close it. You must pick the port from the browser’s dialog. The page cannot open one on its own. A tile is missing from the chain In order of how often it turns out to be the cause: A cable not fully clicked home. The commonest fault by a distance. A missing terminator. Both ends of the chain need one. Without them a chain often works on the bench and fails on a longer cable. Two terminators in the wrong places — for example a plug and the main module’s termination jumper at the same end. A damaged cable. Swap it with a known-good one. Check Diagnose → Counters. A tile accumulating checksum errors or missed replies is a wiring or termination problem. A tile that never appears at all is more likely a cable or a dead board. A key does nothing Is it bound? An unbound key registers nowhere. Check Configure. Does the tile see it at all? Diagnose shows presses straight off the bus, before binding. If it shows there and not in the Driver Station, the problem is the binding or the Driver Station. If it does not show there, it is the switch. Hot-swap sockets: pull the switch and look at the pins. A bent pin folds under the switch instead of entering the socket. Buttons stick on, or fire on their own A worn microswitch chattering — raise that tile’s debounce. If every button on a tile misbehaves at once, suspect the bus rather than the switches: check the counters, the cable and the terminators. Is the board sending my presses at all? The main module’s small RGB light flashes white each time a button is pressed, as the board sends it over USB. That works in every personality, xinput included, so it answers “is it the board or the Driver Station” without a laptop. Flashes, but the Driver Station sees nothing: the board is fine. Check the personality and the Driver Station’s own settings. No flash: the key is not bound, the tile is lost, or the board is in bind mode. Check Configure. Never flashes at all: it may be turned off. It is the Status light checkbox on the Connect screen. The Driver Station sees the wrong thing FRC expects frc; FTC expects xinput. Check on the Connect screen. A personality change only takes effect at a USB reset. Unplug and plug back in. Under FTC, bind the pad with Start+A or Start+B as usual. A key bound as a Start+A or Start+B combo does it in one press (see Binding buttons). Use Diagnose → Test to settle where the problem is: it makes the board report presses with no tile involved. If the Driver Station sees those, everything from the board to the laptop is fine and the problem is on the bus or in the bindings. LEDs are dimmer than I set them That is the power budget working as intended. The board lowers global brightness until the panel fits the current it can draw from USB. Diagnose → Power shows the budget, the worst case and the brightness in use. Raise the budget if the port genuinely supplies more. If the panel cannot fit even at minimum brightness, the LEDs are held off and a fault is raised — the same view says so. My configuration disappeared It was probably never saved. Changes work immediately but live in RAM until Save is pressed. Unplugging before that discards them. Everything worked yesterday Check firmware versions on Connect and Diagnose. A tile updated to firmware the main module does not understand is reported as incompatible rather than being used — the board tells you instead of behaving strangely.
